sentences.text: If you only steer the front wheels of a long truck, you have a truck that cannot turn tight.
But the long body cannot pivot, so its tail swings out wide toward a post.
The swinging tail clips the post and knocks it flat, which in a tight street means a crunched bumper.
So you bolt a steering motor onto the rear axle, so the back wheels can turn too.
At a crawl, the motor turns the rear wheels against the front ones, so the truck pivots in a tight circle like a compact.
A Mercedes S-Class turns its rear wheels up to 10 degrees, which cuts its turning circle by up to about 2 meters.
But at highway speed, turning the rear wheels against the front makes the tail whip around.
So above about 37 mph the rear wheels turn the same way as the front, and the truck tracks straight.
Turning the same way is called in-phase steering, and the tight low-speed turn is called counter-phase.
But if the motor fails, the rod can snap and leave the rear wheels stuck, so the truck veers.
So you add a spring that pulls the rear wheels back to center and holds them straight.
And four-wheel steering is not four-wheel drive, even though all four wheels seem to be doing something.
It only swivels the wheels left and right, and Honda offered it on its Prelude from 1987.
Add a ceiling light and let the truck crab sideways into the garage.
Congratulations, you have built a truck that parks like a compact car.
